source_text: Ἀλλὰ μὴ τῆς πατρίδος ἐκπέσῃ; Ἀλλὰ πᾶσα ἡ ὑπ' οὐρανὸν πόλις αὐτῷ ἐστιν. Ἀλλὰ μὴ τῆς τρυφῆς αὐτόν τις περικόψῃ καὶ τῆς δορυφορίας; Ἀλλὰ καὶ τούτοις ἅπασι χαίρειν εἰπὼν, ἐν οὐρανῷ πολιτεύεται, καὶ πρὸς τὴν μέλλουσαν ἐπείγεται ζωήν. Κἂν αὐτὴν ἐπιδοῦναι δέῃ τὴν ψυχὴν, καὶ τὸ αἷμα εἰσενεγκεῖν, οὐ παραιτήσεται. Ἐντεῦθεν ὁ τοιοῦτος καὶ τυράννων, καὶ βασιλέων, καὶ δήμων, καὶ πάντων ἐστὶ δυνατώτερός τε καὶ εὐπορώτερος. Καὶ ἵνα μάθῃς ὅτι οὐ κολακεία τὸ λεγόμενον, ἀλλ' ἀληθῶς, οἱ μηδὲν κεκτημένοι, οὗτοι μάλιστα πάντων ἐλευθεροστομεῖν δύναιντ' ἂν, πόσοι πλούσιοι κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν ἦσαν Ἡρώδου; πόσοι δυνάσται; τίς παρῆλθεν εἰς μέσον; τίς ἐπετίμησε τῷ τυράννῳ; τίς ἤμυνεν ἀδικουμένοις τοῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ νόμοις; Τῶν μὲν εὐπόρων οὐδείς· ὁ δὲ πένης καὶ πτωχὸς, ὁ μὴ κλίνην, μήτε τράπεζαν, μήτε στέγην ἔχων, ὁ τῆς ἐρήμου πολίτης Ἰωάννης, οὗτος μόνος καὶ πρῶτος μετὰ παῤῥησίας ἁπάσης τὸν τύραννον ἤλεγχε, καὶ τοὺς μοιχαλίους ἐξεκάλυπτε γάμους, καὶ παρόντων ἁπάντων καὶ ἀκουόντων, τὴν καταδικάζουσαν αὐτὸν ἐξέφερε ψῆφον. Καὶ πρὸ τούτου δὲ πάλιν ὁ μέγας Ἠλίας, τῆς μηλωτῆς μηδὲν κεκτημένος πλέον, τὸν ἀσεβῆ καὶ παράνομον Ἀχαὰβ ἐκεῖνον μόνος ἤλεγξε μετὰ πολλῆς ἀνδρείας, Οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως ἐλευθεροστομεῖν παρασκευάζει, καὶ θαῤῥεῖν ἐν ἅπασι πείθει τοῖς δεινοῖς, καὶ ἀναλώτους ἐργάζεται καὶ ἰσχυροὺς, ὡς τὸ μηδὲν κεκτῆσθαι, μηδὲ περιβολήν τινα πραγμάτων ἔχειν. Ὥστε εἴ τις βούλοιτο πολλὴν κεκτῆσθαι δύναμιν ἀσπασάσθω πενίαν, καταφρονείτω τῆς παρούσης ζωῆς, μηδὲν εἶναι νομιζέτω θάνατον. Οὗτος οὐχὶ τῶν εὐπόρων μόνον, οὐδὲ τῶν ἀρχόντων, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτῶν τῶν βασιλευόντων πλείονα τὰς Ἐκκλησίας ὠφελῆσαι δυνήσεται. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ βασιλεύοντες καὶ οἱ εὔποροι, ὅσα ἂν ποιήσωσιν, ἀπὸ χρημάτων ποιοῦσιν· ὁ δὲ τοιοῦτος πολλάκις καὶ ἀπὸ κινδύνων καὶ ἀπὸ θανάτων πολλὰ καὶ μεγάλα συνετέλεσεν. Ὅσῳ δὲ χρυσίου παντὸς τιμιώτερον αἷμα, τοσούτῳ βελτίων ἐκείνης αὕτη ἡ εἰσφορά. εʹ. Τοιοῦτοί τινες ἦσαν καὶ οὗτοι οἱ Παύλου ξενοδόχοι, ἡ Πρίσκιλλα καὶ ὁ Ἀκύλας, οἳ χρημάτων μὲν περιουσίαν οὐκ εἶχον, πλούτου δὲ παντὸς εὐπορωτέραν ἐκέκτηντο γνώμην, καθ' ἑκάστην ἀποθανεῖσθαι προσδοκῶντες ἡμέραν, καὶ ἐν σφαγαῖς καὶ αἵμασι ζῶντες, καὶ διὰ παντὸς μαρτυροῦντες τοῦ χρόνου. Διὰ τοῦτο ἤνθει τὰ ἡμέτερα κατὰ τοὺς καιροὺς ἐκείνους, ὅτι οὕτω μὲν οἱ μαθηταὶ τοῖς διδασκάλοις, οὕτω δὲ οἱ διδάσκαλοι συνεδέδεντο τοῖς μαθηταῖς. Οὐ γὰρ δὴ περὶ τούτων μόνον φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ ἑτέρων πολλῶν. Καὶ γὰρ Ἑβραίοις καὶ Θεσσαλονικεῦσι γράφων καὶ Γαλάταις, πολλὴν ἅπασι μαρτυρεῖ πειρασμῶν ἐπαγωγὴν, καὶ δείκνυσι δι' ὧν ἐπέστελλεν, ὅτι καὶ ἠλαύνοντο καὶ τῆς πατρίδος ἐξέπιπτον, καὶ τὰς οὐσίας ἀπώλλυον, καὶ μέχρις αὐτοῦ τοῦ αἵματος ἐκινδύνευον· καὶ ἅπας ἐναγώνιος αὐτοῖς ὁ βίος ἦν, καὶ αὐτὰ δὲ ἀκρωτηριασθῆναι τὰ μέλη οὐκ ἂν ὑπὲρ τῶν διδασκάλων παρῃτήσαντο. Τοῖς γοῦν Γαλάταις ἐπιστέλλων ἔλεγε· Μαρτυρῶ γὰρ ὑμῖν, ὅτι, εἰ δυνατὸν, τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὑμῶν ἐξορύξαντες ἂν ἐδώκατέ μοι. Καὶ τὸν Ἐπαφρᾶν δὲ τὸν ἐν Κολοσσαῖς ἐπὶ τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἀποδέχεται πάλιν, εἰπὼν, ὅτι Ἠσθένησε παραπλήσιον θανάτου, καὶ ἠλέησεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς, οὐκ αὐτὸν δὲ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμὲ, ἵνα μὴ λύπην ἐπὶ λύπῃ σχῶ.
thought_title: Poverty as the Source of Boldness
orientation: Chrysostom is continuing his praise of the poor man's freedom, now arguing that poverty makes one bolder than kings and tyrants, and citing John the Baptist and Elijah as examples.
pass_a_gloss: But lest he fall out of his fatherland? But every city under heaven is his. But lest someone cut him off from luxury and from bodyguard? But having bid farewell to all these things, he lives as a citizen in heaven, and he presses on toward the life to come. And if he must hand over his very soul, and bring in his blood, he will not refuse. Hence such a man is more powerful and more resourceful than tyrants, and kings, and peoples, and all. And so that you may learn that what is said is not flattery, but truly, those who possess nothing, these most of all would be able to speak freely, how many rich men were there in the time of Herod? how many rulers? who came forward into the midst? who rebuked the tyrant? who defended the wronged laws of God? Of the wealthy no one; but the poor man and beggar, the one having neither bed, nor table, nor roof, the citizen of the desert John, this man alone and foremost with all boldness rebuked the tyrant, and exposed the adulterous marriage, and while all were present and listening, he brought out the vote condemning him. And before this again the great Elijah, possessing nothing more than the sheepskin, alone rebuked that impious and lawless Ahab with much courage. For nothing so prepares one to speak freely, and persuades one to be confident in all dangers, and makes men unconsumed and strong, as possessing nothing, and having no entanglement of affairs. So if anyone should wish to possess much power, let him embrace poverty, let him despise the present life, let him consider death to be nothing. This man will be able to benefit the churches more than not only the wealthy, nor only the rulers, but also than those who are kings themselves. For those who are kings and the wealthy, whatever they may do, they do from money; but such a man often accomplished many and great things both from dangers and from deaths. And by as much as blood is more precious than all gold, by so much is this contribution better than that one. 5. Such were also these hosts of Paul, Priscilla and Aquila, who did not have abundance of possessions, but possessed a disposition richer than all wealth, expecting to die each day, and living amid slaughters and blood, and bearing witness through all time. For this reason our affairs flourished in those times, because thus the disciples were bound to the teachers, and thus the teachers to the disciples. For Paul speaks not about these only, but also about many others. For writing to the Hebrews and Thessalonians and Galatians, he bears witness to all of much onslaught of trials, and he shows through what he wrote, that they were being driven out and were falling out of their fatherland, and were losing their possessions, and were in danger even to their very blood; and their whole life was full of struggle, and they would not have refused even to have their very limbs mutilated for the teachers. Writing to the Galatians, at any rate, he said: For I bear witness to you, that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. And he accepts Epaphras in Colossae again for the same things, saying, that He was sick near to death, and God had mercy on him, and not on him only, but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.

choices.why: πρῶτος here marks John as chief or preeminent in boldness, not first in a temporal sequence
ἀνάλωτος means 'not used up, not worn away'; poverty keeps a man from being consumed by circumstances
περιβολή here is a wrapping or net of business concerns that entangles, not a garment
ἀσπάζομαι means to welcome or embrace gladly, fitting the exhortation to choose poverty
ἐπαγωγή means a bringing upon, an assault of trials, stronger than mere 'coming'
ἐναγώνιος means 'in the midst of contest', describing a life of continual conflict

pass_b_english: But what if he should be driven from his homeland? Every city under heaven is his homeland. But what if someone should cut off his luxury and his retinue? He has said farewell to all these things, and he lives as a citizen of heaven, pressing on toward the life to come. And if he must surrender his very soul and pour out his blood, he will not refuse. From this, such a man is more powerful and more resourceful than tyrants, kings, crowds, and everyone else. And so that you may learn that what I am saying is not flattery but truth: those who possess nothing are the ones most able to speak freely. How many rich men were there in the time of Herod? How many rulers? Who stepped forward? Who rebuked the tyrant? Who defended the laws of God when they were being violated? None of the wealthy did. But the poor and destitute man, the one who had no bed, no table, no roof—John, the citizen of the desert—he alone, foremost in all boldness, was rebuking the tyrant and exposing his adulterous marriage, and in the presence and hearing of all he pronounced the verdict that condemned him. And before him again, the great Elijah, who possessed nothing more than a sheepskin, alone rebuked that impious and lawless Ahab with great courage. For nothing so prepares a man to speak freely, and persuades him to be confident in all dangers, and makes him invulnerable and strong, as possessing nothing and having no entanglement of affairs. So if anyone wishes to possess great power, let him embrace poverty, let him despise this present life, let him consider death to be nothing. Such a man will be able to benefit the churches more than not only the wealthy and the rulers, but even those who reign as kings. For kings and the wealthy, whatever they do, they do from their money; but such a man has often accomplished many great things from dangers and from deaths. And as much as blood is more precious than all gold, so much better is this contribution than that one.

Such were these hosts of Paul, Priscilla and Aquila. They did not have an abundance of money, but they possessed a disposition richer than all wealth, expecting to die each day, living amid slaughter and blood, and bearing witness through all their time. For this reason our affairs flourished in those days, because the disciples were bound to their teachers in this way, and the teachers to their disciples in this way. For Paul speaks not only about these two, but also about many others. Writing to the Hebrews, the Thessalonians, and the Galatians, he bears witness to all of them of a great onslaught of trials, and he shows through his letters that they were being driven out and cast from their homeland, losing their property, and facing danger even to the point of blood. Their whole life was full of struggle, and they would not have refused even to have their own limbs mutilated for their teachers. Writing to the Galatians, he said: "I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me" (Galatians 4:15). And he commends Epaphras, the one in Colossae, again for the same things, saying that he was sick near to death, and God had mercy on him—and not only on him, but also on me, so that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27).

problems.why: The Epaphras quotation is from Colossians 4:12-13 or Philemon 23, not Philippians 2:27 (which refers to Epaphroditus).
"Unconsumed" means not destroyed by fire; ἀναλώτους here means unassailable, invulnerable, or unconquerable.
problems.ruling: ἀναλώτους means 'unconquerable/invulnerable'; 'unconsumed' wrongly implies fire, changing meaning.

fixed: Changed 'unconsumed' to 'invulnerable' because ἀναλώτους here means unassailable or invulnerable, not unconsumed by fire.
Changed the parenthetical reference from Philippians 2:27 to Colossians 4:12-13 because the Epaphras quotation is from Colossians, not Philippians (which refers to Epaphroditus).

last_rejected.why: πένης means poor, not destitute; glossary bans 'destitution' for πενία.
last_rejected.ruling: πτωχὸς means destitute; 'poor and destitute' covers both terms. πένης alone is poor, but paired with πτωχὸς, 'destitute' applies to the latter.

last_rejected.fix: he is being trained as a citizen of heaven
last_rejected.ruling: πολιτεύεται is middle voice present, 'conducts himself as citizen' or 'lives as citizen'; 'lives as a citizen of heaven' is within normal range, not weakened.

last_rejected.quote: he was sick near to death
last_rejected.why: παραπλήσιον θανάτου means 'close to death' or 'near death', not 'sick near to death'—the Greek emphasizes the proximity to death itself, not sickness near death

last_rejected.ruling: Ἠσθένησε ('was sick') + παραπλήσιον θανάτου ('near death') = 'sick near to death'; meaning fully preserved.
